clean_story:
"Wooden giants. Silent carbon vaults.
The word tree comes from Old English ‘trēow,’ meaning a tall plant with a single wooden stem, a name that mirrors its towering, enduring nature.

Most see trees as static pillars of forests, yet their unseen labor is constant: a single oak can absorb 48 pounds of carbon dioxide per year, turning it into wood and oxygen through photosynthesis. Their roots act like straws, pulling water and nutrients from deep underground, while leaves capture sunlight to fuel this process. Some, like the baobab, store thousands of liters of water in their trunks, surviving droughts where other plants wither. Others, like the quaking aspen, form vast networks through shared roots, creating clones that can span miles. Trees do not just stand; they engineer ecosystems, dropping leaves to enrich soil, providing shade that cools the air by up to 10 Farhenheit, and housing entire worlds in their branches.

Three related subjects are root systems, forest canopies and seed dispersal."
